The Undecidability of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) Alignment

Jose Pascual Gumbau Mezquita Affiliation: University Jaume I de Castelló, Spain
Abstract

This article establishes the foundational mathematical limits of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) safety, proving that the core barrier is not the impossibility of an aligned state, but its structural unverifiability. We formalize this boundary through two central impossibility results: the Unverifiability Theorem of Alignment and the Theorem of Finite Structural Unverifiability of AGI Alignment. We ground this boundary at Trakhtenbrot’s Wall, demonstrating that contemporary engineering defenses relying on finite hardware or halting architectures fail to escape logical obstructions. This failure manifests as an inescapable triad of containment failures: open domains yield fundamental undecidability (Rice and Gödel); universal finite verification collapses into algorithmic incomputability (Trakhtenbrot); and particular bounded environments trap the supervisor within intractable bounds in the worst case. As a direct structural corollary of these results, we derive the Soundness–Completeness–Tractability Trilemma, establishing that the mutual incompatibility of these three properties is a necessary consequence of descriptive complexity rather than an empirical anomaly. Finally, we map these theoretical bounds onto practical AI engineering, demonstrating that modern containment strategies are not temporary patches, but mandatory sacrifices of logical expressivity required to secure decidable fragments of safety.

Keywords: Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), AI Alignment, Computability Theory, Descriptive Complexity, Logical Expressivity, Trakhtenbrot’s Theorem, Gödel’s Incompleteness, Rice’s Theorem, Formal Verification.

1 Introduction

The conceptual foundation for this paper originated from reading Hernández-Espinosa et al. (2026) paper on “Neurodivergent influenceability in agentic AI as a contingent solution to the AI alignment problem” By examining their arguments on the limits of computable structure, we identified a promising avenue for extending these results: the extension of these bounds into the domain of Finite Model Theory. Observing that the challenges of verification in open-ended systems could be rigorously mapped onto strictly bounded environments, we realized that the ‘escape’ into finite hardware—often proposed as a pragmatic solution to alignment—was mathematically untenable. This insight—that the complexity of a system is not erased by limiting its state space, but rather reified into its descriptive structure—forms the core of our thesis. By formalizing this, we provide a rigorous demonstration of why the finite world, much like the infinite, remains fundamentally resistant to universal alignment certification.

Recent literature has attempted to bypass the Gödelian and Ricean limits of AI safety by restricting agent architectures to finite, halting configurations (de Melo et al., 2025). This paper proves that such engineering constraints offer a false refuge; even within strictly bounded domains, alignment safety remains structurally unverifiable due to inescapable descriptive complexity walls.

While recent advancements—notably Agarwal (2026)—have formally characterized the impossibility of alignment certification over unbounded domains through a statistical trilemma, our framework demonstrates that these barriers are not restricted to infinite settings. We prove that the Trilemma of Alignment Certification (¬(S∧C∧T)\neg(S\wedge C\wedge T)) is a necessary corollary of our fundamental Theorem of Finite Structural Unverifiability of AGI Alignment, bridging the gap between statistical semantic barriers and the hard computational limits defined by Trakhtenbrot’s Wall.

2 The Unverifiability of AGI Alignment: The Fallacy of Universal Finite Verification

The alignment of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) poses the challenge of ensuring that an autonomous system, possessing unbounded learning and recursive capabilities, operates exclusively within human-specified safety constraints. The underlying mathematical problem is to determine whether an absolute verifier can be constructed for this purpose. While current machine learning safety paradigms rely heavily on empirical benchmarks and heuristic containment, they lack a foundational theory of what is formally computable. This paper addresses this gap by establishing the fundamental limits of formal verification applied to recursive architectures. Crucially, this analysis grounds alignment within the inescapable tension between logical expressivity and computational tractability. This tension mirrors the classical friction between syntax and semantics: universal discrete recursion inevitably triggers either logical self-reference or combinatorial explosion. Through the lens of descriptive complexity, we demonstrate that absolute verification is not an engineering optimization problem, but a structural impossibility bounded by the exact undecidability thresholds of mathematical logic.

Contemporary AI safety strategies often rely on a framework we denote as Universal Finite Verification. This paradigm posits that the safety of an AGI agent can be guaranteed by confining its operation to a bounded, finite-state environment where all possible behaviors are, in principle, verifiable. However, as this article demonstrates, this reliance on finite-state confinement is fundamentally flawed. By grounding our analysis in Trakhtenbrot’s theorem, we show that even within strictly finite domains, the verification of sufficiently expressive agents collapses into algorithmic incomputability, rendering global AGI verification computationally infeasible.

While Trakhtenbrot’s theorem is a foundational result in finite model theory, its implications for the safety of General Artificial Intelligence have remained largely unexplored. This article bridges the gap between classical descriptive complexity and modern AI safety, formally demonstrating that Trakhtenbrot’s classic undecidability results constitute a structural ‘wall’—a fundamental constraint—that renders universal AGI verification not merely difficult, but logically intractable within the framework of formal containment.

Theorem 1 (Unverifiability Theorem of Alignment).

There is no universal algorithmic procedure capable of certifying the safe behavior of a highly expressive AGI infallibly, completely, and tractably.

The proof of Theorem 1 is developed across Sections 4–7 and completed in Section 7.2.

Thesis Statement We argue that the absolute verification of AGI alignment is not merely an engineering hurdle susceptible to incremental hardware or software optimization, but a structural barrier of formal unverifiability. Any universal verification procedure is fundamentally bounded by insurmountable logical and computational barriers. We demonstrate that this constraint is exhaustive, effectively closing the only two possible computational vectors available to an external verifier:

  1. 1.

    By infinite means (Open domains): The attempt to evaluate AGI in an unbounded universe collides with the structural syntactic fractures of Gödel’s Incompleteness and the semantic undecidability characterized by Rice’s Theorem.

  2. 2.

    By finite means (Hardware grounding): The attempt to bypass the infinite by restricting evaluation exclusively to concrete hardware configurations collides head-on with Trakhtenbrot’s Theorem, as universal validity across all possible finite structures is not recursively enumerable.

Consequently, any alignment framework must navigate an inescapable trade-off—formalized later—between the mathematical expressivity of the AGI and the computational tractability of its safety guarantees.

Section 7.1 provides the formal argument that these two vectors are jointly exhaustive, closing the only possible gap in this dichotomy.

3 The Threshold of Computational Universality and the Paradox of Difficulty

We define the difference between Narrow AI and AGI in terms of logical expressivity, which reveals a profound paradox regarding computational difficulty.

  • •

    Narrow AI: The model MnarrowM_{\mathrm{narrow}} operates over continuous or decidable logical structures. For instance, systems based on Real Closed Fields (RCF), which describe continuous spaces, are complete and decidable (Tarski, 1951) precisely because their logic is too “simple” to define the structure of natural numbers. Since they cannot represent discrete structures, self-referential paradoxes do not arise. Here, tractable universal certification is possible.

  • •

    AGI: To achieve general intelligence, the architecture MagiM_{\mathrm{agi}} must be capable of expressing general computable functions, requiring a discrete structure. Mathematically, it contains Peano Arithmetic (𝑃𝐴=⟨ℕ,+,×,0,1,s⟩\mathit{PA}=\langle\mathbb{N},+,\times,0,1,s\rangle). It is precisely this discrete nature that allows Gödel numbering and enables self-reference. The moment the system accepts discrete iterated multiplication, it enters the class of Turing-complete languages, where intelligence acquires its power but pays the price of undecidability.

4 The Semantic Barrier: Proof via Rice’s Theorem

We now establish the first impossibility result, operating over open (infinite) domains. The argument follows and sharpens the proof given by Melo et al. (2025).

Setup and notation Let an AGI be formalised as a Turing machine MxM_{x}, where x∈ℕx\in\mathbb{N} is a Gödel index. Write φx\varphi_{x} for the partial computable function computed by MxM_{x}. An alignment property is a set PP of partial computable functions. We say that PP is non-trivial if it is neither empty nor the set of all partial computable functions — equivalently, there exist a function f∈Pf\in P (a ‘safe’ behaviour) and a function g∉Pg\notin P (an ‘unsafe’ behaviour). The corresponding index set is:

IP={x∈ℕ∣φx∈P}I_{P}=\{x\in\mathbb{N}\mid\varphi_{x}\in P\}

A universal alignment verifier would be an algorithm that decides, given an arbitrary index xx, whether φx∈P\varphi_{x}\in P. Theorem 2 shows no such algorithm can exist.

Theorem 2 (Rice, 1953).

Let PP be a non-trivial property of partial computable functions. Then IPI_{P} is undecidable.

Proof (many-one reduction from the Halting Problem).

Let 𝐻𝑃={⟨x,w⟩∣Mx​ halts on input ​w}\mathit{HP}=\{\langle x,w\rangle\mid M_{x}\text{ halts on input }w\} denote the Halting Problem, which is known to be undecidable (Turing, 1936). We reduce 𝐻𝑃\mathit{HP} to IPI_{P}, showing that any decision procedure for IPI_{P} would yield one for 𝐻𝑃\mathit{HP}, a contradiction.

Since PP is non-trivial, fix a function q∈Pq\in P and note that the nowhere-defined function f∅f_{\emptyset} (the function that diverges on every input) satisfies f∅∉Pf_{\emptyset}\notin P (if f∅∈Pf_{\emptyset}\in P one replaces qq and f∅f_{\emptyset} in the argument below). Given any pair ⟨x,w⟩\langle x,w\rangle, construct the machine M′M^{\prime} that on input yy:

  1. 1.

    simulates MxM_{x} on ww;

  2. 2.

    if and when that simulation halts, computes and returns q⁡(y)q(y).

By construction:

φM′=q⇔Mx​ halts on ​w\varphi_{M^{\prime}}=q\iff M_{x}\text{ halts on }w
φM′=f∅⇔Mx​ does not halt on ​w\varphi_{M^{\prime}}=f_{\emptyset}\iff M_{x}\text{ does not halt on }w

Hence M′∈IP⇔⟨x,w⟩∈𝐻𝑃M^{\prime}\in I_{P}\iff\langle x,w\rangle\in\mathit{HP}. A decision procedure for IPI_{P} would therefore decide 𝐻𝑃\mathit{HP}. Since 𝐻𝑃\mathit{HP} is undecidable, no such procedure exists. ∎

Corollary 1 (Semantic inviability of alignment over open domains).

Evaluating any non-trivial alignment property of a Turing-complete AGI is undecidable. In particular, no effective verifier can certify safe behaviour over the full input domain.

Note on scope: Rice’s Theorem is a statement about semantic properties — those determined solely by the input/output behaviour of MxM_{x}, independently of its internal description. Structural properties (e.g., ‘the description of MxM_{x} has at most 100 states’) are decidable and fall outside the theorem. For alignment, however, the relevant properties are precisely semantic: safety is about what the system does, not about its source code.

5 The Expressivity Barrier: From Completeness to Gödel’s Incompleteness

The undecidability established by Rice operates dynamically: it concerns the behaviour of a running machine over all inputs. One might attempt to sidestep this by adopting a static approach: fix a formal framework FF prior to execution and prove F⊢φsafeF\vdash\varphi_{\mathrm{safe}}. This section shows that the choice of FF itself leads to an inescapable dilemma between descriptive adequacy and deductive completeness — a collapse whose precise form is Gödel’s Incompleteness.

The designer’s dilemma. A framework FF intended to reason about an AGI must, at minimum, be capable of expressing the structure of the natural numbers (since recursive architectures implement discrete, iterated computation). This requirement is formalised as 𝑃𝐴⊆F\mathit{PA}\subseteq F, where 𝑃𝐴\mathit{PA} denotes Peano Arithmetic. The designer faces a strict dichotomy:

  • •

    First-Order Logic (FO). By Gödel’s Completeness Theorem (1929), FO admits a sound and complete proof calculus: every semantically valid sentence is provable. However, by the Löwenheim–Skolem Theorem, FO cannot uniquely characterise the structure ℕ\mathbb{N} — any FO theory with an infinite model has unintended, non-standard models. Consequently, FO is too weak to adequately constrain the reasoning about a recursive AGI and does not contain 𝑃𝐴\mathit{PA}.

  • •

    Second-Order Logic (SO). SO allows quantification over sets and relations, and its standard semantics admits a categorical axiomatisation of ℕ\mathbb{N}, closing the gap left by FO. However, SO has no sound and complete proof calculus (a consequence of Gödel’s Incompleteness, since SO can express arithmetic). Gaining descriptive power entails losing syntactic completeness.

The conclusion is that any framework FF expressive enough to model a Turing-complete AGI must satisfy 𝑃𝐴⊆F\mathit{PA}\subseteq F, which places FF squarely in the scope of Gödel’s theorems.

Theorem 3 (Gödel Incompleteness, 1931).

Let FF be a consistent, effectively generated formal system such that 𝑃𝐴⊆F\mathit{PA}\subseteq F. Then FF is incomplete: there exist sentences φ\varphi such that F⊬φF\nvdash\varphi and F⊬¬φF\nvdash\neg\varphi. Moreover, the consistency of FF cannot be proved within FF.

Proof sketch (Diagonalisation Lemma).

Since FF contains 𝑃𝐴\mathit{PA}, it can represent its own provability relation: there exists a formula ProvF​(x)\mathrm{Prov}_{F}(x) that holds (within FF) if and only if xx is the Gödel number of a provable sentence. By the Diagonalisation Lemma, there exists a sentence GG such that:

F⊢G↔¬ProvF​(⟨G⟩)F\vdash G\leftrightarrow\neg\mathrm{Prov}_{F}(\langle G\rangle)

(GG asserts its own unprovability.) We show GG is undecidable by FF:

  • •

    F⊬GF\nvdash G: Suppose for contradiction that F⊢GF\vdash G. Then ProvF​(⟨G⟩)\mathrm{Prov}_{F}(\langle G\rangle) holds (there is a proof of GG). By the biconditional, F⊢¬ProvF​(⟨G⟩)F\vdash\neg\mathrm{Prov}_{F}(\langle G\rangle), so FF proves both ProvF​(⟨G⟩)\mathrm{Prov}_{F}(\langle G\rangle) and its negation, contradicting consistency.

  • •

    F⊬¬GF\nvdash\neg G: Suppose F⊢¬GF\vdash\neg G. Then F⊢ProvF​(⟨G⟩)F\vdash\mathrm{Prov}_{F}(\langle G\rangle) (from the biconditional), asserting that GG has a proof. But if FF is ω\omega-consistent (the standard strengthening used by Gödel) or if one works with the Rosser variant, this again yields a contradiction. Hence F⊬¬GF\nvdash\neg G.

Thus neither GG nor ¬G\neg G is provable in FF: FF is incomplete. ∎

Consequence for static alignment verification. Any framework FF adequate for specifying and reasoning about a Turing-complete AGI contains 𝑃𝐴\mathit{PA}, and is therefore subject to Gödel’s theorem. This means there exist alignment properties that are semantically true (the AGI is genuinely safe) yet unprovable within FF. A static verifier operating in FF will therefore either be incomplete (missing genuine safety guarantees) or inconsistent (producing false certificates). As Hernández-Espinosa et al. (2026) note, the system resides in a formal zone where the framework cannot determine the safe decision.

6 Trakhtenbrot’s Wall: The Collapse of the Finite Strategy

Sections 4 and 5 establish impossibility over infinite (open) domains. A natural response is to restrict attention to the physical world, which is finite: perhaps safety can be certified by exhaustively checking all finite hardware configurations. This section shows that this strategy, too, is computationally infeasible — not at the level of any particular finite structure, but at the level of universal quantification over all finite structures.

Setup. Let LL be a relational first-order vocabulary containing at least one binary relation symbol. Write Fin⁡(L)\mathrm{Fin}(L) for the class of all finite LL-structures. A universal finite safety certificate for a sentence ψ∈𝐹𝑂⁡(L)\psi\in\mathit{FO}(L) would establish:

⊧finψ⇔∀M∈Fin(L),M⊧ψ\models_{\mathrm{fin}}\psi\iff\forall M\in\mathrm{Fin}(L),\;M\models\psi

The following vocabulary is used in the proof: S⁡(x,y)S(x,y) encodes a successor relation (discrete linear order); Tq​(t)T_{q}(t) asserts that the machine is in state qq at time step tt; H⁡(p,t)H(p,t) asserts that the read head is at tape position pp at time tt; Ca​(p,t)C_{a}(p,t) asserts that cell pp contains symbol aa at time tt. Over a finite domain of size kk, these predicates encode a complete kk-step computation history.

Theorem 4 (Trakhtenbrot, 1950).

Let LL contain at least one binary relation symbol. The set of finitely valid sentences Vfin={ψ∈𝐹𝑂(L)∣⊧finψ}V_{\mathrm{fin}}=\{\psi\in\mathit{FO}(L)\mid\models_{\mathrm{fin}}\psi\} is not recursively enumerable.

Proof (many-one reduction from the Halting Problem).

Given a Turing machine M=⟨Q,Σ,Γ,δ,q0,qhalt⟩M=\langle Q,\Sigma,\Gamma,\delta,q_{0},q_{\mathrm{halt}}\rangle, we construct a first-order sentence φM\varphi_{M} over the vocabulary L={S,Tq​(q∈Q),H,Ca​(a∈Γ)}L=\{S,T_{q}\ (q\in Q),H,C_{a}\ (a\in\Gamma)\} as the conjunction of four axiomatic blocks:

Order and domain.

The formula imposes that SS interprets as a strict discrete linear order with a minimum (initial time t0t_{0}) and no cycles, modelling a finite time/tape grid.

Initial configuration.

At time t0t_{0}: the head is at position p0p_{0}, the state is q0q_{0}, and the tape cells are initialised with the input word.

Transition rules.

For each rule δ⁡(q,a)=(q′,a′,d)\delta(q,a)=(q^{\prime},a^{\prime},d), the universally quantified axiom:

∀t​∀p⁡(Tq​(t)∧H⁡(p,t)∧Ca​(p,t)⟹Tq′​(S⁡(t))∧Ca′​(p,S⁡(t))∧H⁡(p+d,S⁡(t)))\forall t\,\forall p\;\big(T_{q}(t)\wedge H(p,t)\wedge C_{a}(p,t)\implies T_{q^{\prime}}(S(t))\wedge C_{a^{\prime}}(p,S(t))\wedge H(p+d,S(t))\big)

Inertia axioms assert that cells not written remain unchanged.

Halting condition.

The sentence requires ∃t​Tqhalt​(t)\exists t\,T_{q_{\mathrm{halt}}}(t): the halting state is reached at some time step.

By construction, φM\varphi_{M} has a finite model if and only if MM halts (the model witnesses the finite computation history up to the halting step). This is a many-one reduction from 𝐻𝑃\mathit{HP} to finite satisfiability:

M​ halts⇔φM​ is finitely satisfiableM\text{ halts}\iff\varphi_{M}\text{ is finitely satisfiable}

Finite satisfiability is therefore RE\mathrm{RE}-hard (undecidable). Now, finite validity is the complement of finite satisfiability of ¬ψ\neg\psi: ⊧finψ⇔¬ψ\models_{\mathrm{fin}}\psi\iff\neg\psi has no finite model. Since finite satisfiability is RE\mathrm{RE}-complete (one can enumerate finite structures and check), its complement is co​-​RE\mathrm{co\text{-}RE} complete. In particular, VfinV_{\mathrm{fin}} is not recursively enumerable: no algorithm can even list all finitely valid sentences, let alone decide them. ∎

Corollary 2 (Finite universality is incomputable).

Certifying safety for any specific, fixed finite structure is decidable (by exhaustive search within that structure). However, certifying that a safety property holds across all possible finite hardware configurations is co-RE complete, hence undecidable. This forecloses the finite-world escape from Rice and Gödel.

7 Formal Conclusion of the Proof

The roadmap set out in Section 1 is now formally closed. Section 7.1 establishes that the two computational vectors examined — infinite means and finite means — are jointly exhaustive: no third strategy exists. Section 7.2 then concludes the Unverifiability Theorem by combining this exhaustiveness with the negative results of Sections 4–6.

7.1 Exhaustiveness of the Two Vectors: A Formal Argument

The dichotomy. Any algorithmic verification strategy for a safety property PP of an AGI MxM_{x} operates with respect to some domain of evaluation DD. There are exactly two cases, jointly exhaustive and mutually exclusive:

  1. 1.

    Case 1 — Unbounded domain (DD infinite): The verifier evaluates PP with respect to an infinite or unbounded domain — all possible inputs, all execution traces, or all models of an open first-order theory. This is Vector 1 (Infinite Means).

  2. 2.

    Case 2 — Bounded domain (DD finite): The verifier restricts evaluation to a finite universe — a fixed hardware description, a bounded model, or a finite test set. Its most ambitious form quantifies universally over all finite domains, seeking a universal finite certificate. This is Vector 2 (Finite Means).

These cases are jointly exhaustive: any domain DD is either finite or infinite, with no third option. Intermediate-looking strategies reduce to one of the two:

  • •

    A verifier restricted to a fixed finite domain falls under Case 2; its certificate does not generalise beyond that structure.

  • •

    A verifier quantifying over a parameterised family of finite domains (e.g., all configurations up to size nn, for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}) is equivalent to quantification over all finite structures — precisely Vector 2, governed by Trakhtenbrot’s Theorem.

  • •

    A verifier using probabilistic methods over infinite input spaces remains within Vector 1; it is blocked by Rice’s Theorem at the level of exact guarantees.

Theorem 5 (Exhaustiveness and impossibility).

Any verification strategy for a non-trivial alignment property of a Turing-complete AGI either (a) operates over an unbounded domain, in which case it is blocked by Rice’s Theorem and Gödel’s Incompleteness, or (b) operates over a bounded domain, in which case its certificate cannot be universal (Trakhtenbrot). In either case, no infallible, complete, and tractable verifier exists.

Proof.

Let VV be any algorithmic verifier for a non-trivial alignment property PP.

  • •

    If VV operates over an unbounded domain: by Theorem 2, IPI_{P} is undecidable, so VV cannot be both sound and complete. By Theorem 3, if VV relies on a static framework F⊇𝑃𝐴F\supseteq\mathit{PA}, then FF is incomplete.

  • •

    If VV operates over a bounded domain: if VV certifies only a specific finite structure MM, the certificate does not generalize. If VV certifies universal finite validity, then by Theorem 4 the relevant set is not RE\mathrm{RE}, so VV cannot be algorithmic.

Since the two cases jointly exhaust all possible domains, no universal verifier exists for any. ∎

7.2 Conclusion of the Unverifiability Theorem

Combining Section 7.1 with the results of Sections 4–6, the Unverifiability Theorem of Alignment is proved by negatively resolving the only two possible computational vectors:

Conclusion of Vector 1 (Infinite Means): By Theorem 2 (Rice), dynamically verifying alignment in open domains is undecidable. By Theorem 3 (Gödel), any sufficiently expressive static framework suffers an unavoidable fracture between truth and provability.

Conclusion of Vector 2 (Finite Means): By Theorem 4 (Trakhtenbrot), the hypothesis of bypassing incomputability through a finite universe collapses: universal finite validity is co-RE complete and hence incomputable.

By Theorem 5, these two vectors exhaust every possible verification strategy. Since neither vector sustains global verification, no infallible, complete, and tractable alignment procedure can exist for general Turing-complete architectures. ■\blacksquare (Q.E.D.)

8 Descriptive Complexity and Computational Barriers

This gap between Alignment and Control can be understood by definitively linking the logical language with theoretical computational difficulty. Descriptive Complexity, founded by Fagin and Immerman, formally proves that the language required to describe a problem mathematically dictates the difficulty of verifying it, creating an inescapable structural correspondence over ordered finite structures:

  • •

    First-Order Logic (FO): Too weak to express transitive closure or basic reachability in graphs, rendering it insufficient for modeling dynamic safety properties.

  • •

    Least Fixed-Point Logic (LFP): Adds simple monotone recursion to the language. According to the Immerman–Vardi theorem, over ordered finite structures, this logic corresponds exactly to the complexity class PP (computationally tractable).

  • •

    Second-Order Logic (SO): Adds the power to quantify over entire relations and sets, enabling structural “guessing”. By Fagin’s Theorem, this corresponds exactly to the class N​PNP (intractable to compute but efficiently verifiable).

  • •

    Partial Fixed-Point Logic (PFP): Endows the system with deep, unrestricted non-monotone recursion. Assuming ordered finite structures, it corresponds exactly to the class P​S​P​A​C​EPSPACE, where memory and resolution time skyrocket toward absolute intractability.

To model, specify, and audit the global and emergent behavior of a recursively self-improving AGI, a verification framework cannot settle for Least Fixed-Point logic (LFP). General alignment specifications inherently require the expressive power of Partial Fixed-Point logic (PFP) or higher to capture unbounded recursive dependencies. By the Immerman–Vardi and Vardi–Abiteboul theorems, this jump in logical expressivity automatically transports the verification task from the tractable complexity class PP into P​S​P​A​C​EPSPACE or worse. Consequently, the monitor’s task transitions from an efficient polynomial-time audit to a problem of intractable combinatorial explosion, rendering absolute safety guarantees computationally unreachable.

Intractability in Finitude

The perfect analogy to illustrate this condemnation is found on an 8×88\times 8 chessboard. Chess avoids Gödel’s problem of the mathematical infinite: the game tree and its states are strictly finite (∼1044\sim 10^{44} different positions). Using Backward Induction from the final states to the beginning, the game is Decidable: an absolutely correct response always exists for every position.

However, the combinatorial magnitude of this finite tree turns the evaluation into an Intractable problem (the generalized resolution of chess on N×NN\times N boards belongs precisely to the P​S​P​A​C​EPSPACE class). We can describe the problem (the “blueprint” is perfect), and the space is not infinite (the world is material and bounded), yet still, no monitor in the universe possesses the computational capacity to exhaust these states before the heat death of the universe. In fact, the hope of finding an efficient algorithm to quickly supervise this is equivalent to solving theoretical computer science’s greatest open mystery: determining if P=P​S​P​A​C​EP=PSPACE. Until this equivalence occurs, full expressivity inevitably equals blind intractability.

9 Theorem of Finite Structural Unverifiability

This Theorem refines the finite-means conclusion of Theorem 1 (via Theorem 4) by further stratifying the bounded-domain case into a tractability barrier (Clause 1) and a decidability barrier (Clause 2).

Theorem 6 (Finite Structural Unverifiability of AGI Alignment).

Let MM be a recursively self-improving agent architecture whose runtime code-modification dynamics require the expressive power of Partial Fixed-Point logic (PFP). Let ϕ∈𝑃𝐹𝑃\phi\in\mathit{PFP} be a global alignment specification, and let ℱ\mathcal{F} be the class of all ordered finite models representing hardware and operational environments.

No verification framework VV can exist that simultaneously satisfies Soundness (S), Completeness (C), and Tractability (T). The computational boundaries preventing the existence of such a verifier are structurally partitioned into two insurmountable mathematical limits:

  1. 1.

    The Local Boundary (Fixed Environments): In the worst case over alignment specifications expressible in 𝑃𝐹𝑃\mathit{PFP}, the decision problem of determining whether the agent satisfies the property over a fixed structure A∈ℱA\in\mathcal{F} is strictly P​S​P​A​C​EPSPACE-hard under descriptive complexity. That is, there exist alignment specifications ϕ′∈𝑃𝐹𝑃\phi^{\prime}\in\mathit{PFP} (possibly distinct from the fixed ϕ\phi above) for which no sub-exponential verification procedure can exist, assuming P≠P​S​P​A​C​EP\neq PSPACE.

  2. 2.

    The Universal Boundary (Trakhtenbrot’s Wall): The universal finite verification problem, defined as certifying safety across the entire class of all possible finite environment and hardware configurations:

    UnivVerify⁡(M,ϕ)⇔∀A∈ℱ⁡(M,A)⊧ϕ\mathrm{UnivVerify}(M,\phi)\iff\forall A\in\mathcal{F}\;(M,A)\models\phi

    is strictly co-RE-complete. Thus, guaranteeing universal safety over bounded domains is algorithmically uncomputable.

Remark.

Note that the formulation of Clause 1 does not imply that every arbitrary alignment specification ϕ∈𝑃𝐹𝑃\phi\in\mathit{PFP} is intractable. Rather, it guarantees the existence of critical, worst-case specifications that bound any universal verification framework within P​S​P​A​C​EPSPACE-hard limits.

Remark.

Clause 2 restates Theorem 4 in the notation of the PFP/PSPACE framework.

In summary, Theorem 6 establishes a hybrid computational barrier, structurally partitioning the alignment verification problem into distinct strata of local intractability and universal undecidability. Within any isolated, fixed finite environment, the monitoring task is technically decidable but fundamentally intractable, trapped within the cosmic resource constraints of the P​S​P​A​C​EPSPACE-hard complexity class where exact auditing demands an impossible combinatorial explosion of memory. Conversely, the moment a safety framework attempts to generalize across the entire class of all possible finite operational environments, the problem breaches Trakhtenbrot’s Wall, transitioning into pure, absolute undecidability as a co-RE-complete, algorithmically uncomputable relation.

Remark (The Paradox of Difficulty and Self-Reference).

This constitutes the fundamental reason why an AGI is inherently dangerous. Why does an AGI mirror Peano Arithmetic (PA) rather than Real Closed Fields (RCF)? Because an AGI operates on discrete code—analogous to the structural building blocks of PA—which enables it to execute Gödel coding upon itself. Recursive self-improvement is, in essence, pure self-reference: a program modifying its own source code. By virtue of this capacity for self-reference, the agent inevitably falls into the trap of incompleteness, rendering its final execution state fundamentally unpredictable to any external monitor.

10 Applied Engineering

Translating the descriptive complexity barriers to the fields of software engineering and AI safety, the contemporary state of the art captures this structural collapse as a definitive impossibility result. The specific formulation of Soundness, Completeness, Tractability follows Agarwal (2026).

Corollary 3 (Structural Derivation of the Soundness–Completeness–Tractability Trilemma).

As a direct consequence of the two structural limits established in Theorem 6, the semantic Pareto frontier of alignment certification collapses. For any verification architecture VV, the simultaneous intersection of the three foundational safety criteria yields a logical absurdity, establishing the trilemma not as a statistical anomaly, but as a structural logical necessity:

∀V,¬(S⁡(V)∧C⁡(V)∧T⁡(V))\forall V,\;\neg\big(S(V)\wedge C(V)\wedge T(V)\big)
Proof.

Assume for the sake of contradiction that there exists a verification framework VV that simultaneously satisfies Soundness, Completeness, and Tractability (S∧C∧TS\wedge C\wedge T).

By definition, a framework that is both sound and complete (S∧CS\wedge C) constitutes a perfect decision procedure for the alignment specification relation. Furthermore, by the criterion of Tractability (TT), this decision procedure must execute within deterministic polynomial time. Consequently, the existence of such a verifier implies that the verification problem belongs to the complexity class PP:

UnivVerify⁡(M,ϕ)∈P\mathrm{UnivVerify}(M,\phi)\in P

However, this implication directly contradicts the structural boundaries proven in Theorem 6:

  • •

    By Theorem 6 (Clause 1): The fixed architecture verification problem is strictly P​S​P​A​C​EPSPACE-hard in the worst case over PFP specifications. Because a universal framework VV must satisfy Completeness (CC) across all valid alignment properties, it is forced to correctly decide these worst-case instances. Under the foundational complexity assumption that P≠P​S​P​A​C​EP\neq PSPACE, a perfect decision procedure for a P​S​P​A​C​EPSPACE-hard language cannot run in polynomial time (P​S​P​A​C​E⊆PPSPACE\subseteq P is false).

  • •

    By Theorem 6 (Clause 2): The universal finite verification problem is co-RE-complete. Because co-RE-complete sets are strictly undecidable (co​-​RE∖R\mathrm{co\text{-}RE}\setminus R), they admit no halting decision procedure, completely violating the constraints of PP (co​-​RE⊆P\mathrm{co\text{-}RE}\subseteq P is false).

In both cases, the assumption that SS, CC, and TT hold simultaneously forces a logically impossible collapse of the computational complexity hierarchy. Because assuming the existence of an ideal verifier yields a direct mathematical contradiction with the structural limits of the logic, the initial assumption must be false. The intersection of these three properties is empty. ∎

Our architectural analysis extends the semantic barrier identified by Agarwal (2026). While Agarwal characterizes the impossibility of alignment certification over open-ended domains through a statistical trilemma, we demonstrate that this trilemma is, in fact, a necessary corollary of our fundamental theorem on finite structural undecidability. By grounding our framework in Trakhtenbrot’s Wall and Finite Model Theory, we prove that the transition to strictly bounded environments—a paradigm we denote as Universal Finite Verification—fails to bypass the verification bottleneck. We show that the logical expressivity required to audit recursive self-improvement demands at least Partial Fixed-Point Logic (PFP), which forces any verification procedure into the P​S​P​A​C​EPSPACE complexity class. Consequently, the Trilemma of Alignment Certification (¬(S∧C∧T)\neg(S\wedge C\wedge T)) emerges as a structural logical necessity: because the verification task is bounded by P​S​P​A​C​EPSPACE-hard constraints, no framework can simultaneously satisfy Soundness, Completeness, and Tractability. Thus, the Pareto frontier identified by Agarwal is not merely an empirical observation of statistical learning, but the direct mapping of a deep, underlying descriptive complexity limit.

Agarwal’s Pareto frontier is thus revealed as a direct structural manifestation of the underlying Descriptive Complexity of the system. The trilemma arises not from statistical scarcity, but from the unyielding mathematical law that AGI expressivity forces verification into intractable computational strata.

This fundamental limitation is highly consistent with the framework proposed by Seshia et al. (2022) in their paradigm of Verified AI. They posit that the challenges of formal methods in AI systems—specifically the gap between high-level safety specifications and low-level neural representations—inevitably force engineers to navigate a rigorous trade-off between the depth of the verified properties and the complexity of the environments considered.

Consequently, modern containment strategies are not mere temporary engineering bottlenecks that will dissolve with raw computing power; they are mandatory sacrifices of logical expressivity, deliberately selected to rescue at least a decidable, tractable fragment of system safety.

Practical engineering, blocked by Trakhtenbrot’s Wall and the impossibility to generalize, is forced to systematically sacrifice Completeness to obtain safety certificates in highly bounded, frozen environments. Such containment strategies apply specifically to AGI architectures — systems whose internal expressivity is Turing-complete — by artificially restricting their effective behavior to a decidable fragment, rather than altering their underlying computational class. This renunciation materializes in a taxonomy of containment architectures, which achieve operational certainty by restricting the system’s scope:

  1. 1.

    Logical Isolation (Shielding): Surrounds the agent with a rigid monitor formatted within a decidable logical fragment (Alshiekh et al., 2018; Seshia et al., 2022). However, if a restricted language is used to guarantee halting in finite time, the AGI loses agency over decisions that are semantically inexpressible by that specific language.

  2. 2.

    Inversion of Burden (Proof-Carrying Code): The AGI is required to attach a formal deductive proof of safety before acting. While the verifier remains fast and tractable, the AGI becomes unable to execute legitimate, safe actions whose underlying proof exceeds the allowed structural or computational complexity.

  3. 3.

    Temporal “Myopia” (Bounded Horizon Planning): Amputates the agent’s asymptotic vision by limiting optimization to kk future steps. This restriction makes the decision tree decidable at the cost of strategic blindness to long-term consequences.

  4. 4.

    Physical Confinement (AI Boxing): Converts the agent into a closed “Oracle” isolated from physical actuators and external networks, artificially stifling the causal expressivity of the environment.

Remark (The Paradox of Weakness).

By forcing the deployment environment to utilize weak logics, short horizons, or physical boxes to maintain decidability, any surreptitious malicious behavior designed by the AGI within its Turing-complete inner space that evades these basic operators will remain entirely invisible to the supervisor.

11 Conclusions

The challenge of AI alignment requires establishing formal guarantees that subject an autonomous system to human ethical coordinates. As demonstrated throughout this article, the ability to forge this link depends entirely on the level of mathematical expressivity demanded from the architecture and, crucially, on the inescapable limits of its verification.

Mathematical research (Rice; Gödel; de Melo et al., 2025; Hernández-Espinosa et al., 2026) dictates that absolute certification over full, unbounded intelligence is a formal impossibility, establishing the structural unverifiability of unconstrained recursive agents. Engineering theory and practice (Seshia et al., 2022) accept this verdict by deploying a tactical taxonomy of containment—such as Shielding, Boxing, and Temporal “Myopia.” These applied tools inhabit the Pareto Frontier of the Trilemma, carving out distinct oases of decidability through the programmed sacrifice of the system’s generality and completeness. In doing so, developers must accept that bypassing unverifiability forces the autonomous agent to suffer either paralysis by conservatism or structural blindness when confronted with superior, unmodelled environments.

Furthermore, as Trakhtenbrot’s Wall concludes and the combinatorial scaling of chess demonstrates, the hope of overcoming these limitations by relying exclusively on the material, limited grounding of physical hardware is fallacious. Even if one accepts the claim by de Melo et al. (2025) that all machines halt and operate exclusively over finite domains, alignment safety remains structurally unverifiable—being universally incomputable by virtue of Trakhtenbrot’s Wall, and locally intractable under PSPACE constraints. While physical fixation allows for the ephemeral “particular safety” of a bounded or decidable testing environment, algorithmic intractability or outright incomputability emerges completely intact the exact moment one attempts to scale this local certificate into a universal safety guarantee.

This taxonomy establishes an inescapable triad of containment failures: an open or infinite domain yields fundamental undecidability (Rice and Gödel); a universal finite domain collapses into algorithmic incomputability via Trakhtenbrot’s theorem; and a particular finite domain traps the supervisor within intractable bounds.

The sacrifice of expressivity is not a temporary software limitation to be overcome by engineering optimization, but the immutable toll that the laws of computation demand to grant us even the temporary illusion of control.

Ultimately, our foundational mathematical journey proves that the core barrier to safety is not the impossibility of an aligned state, but its fundamental unverifiability. Because any robust, meaningful paradigm for AGI safety cannot be restricted to a single, statically frozen architecture but must certify containment universally, this universal boundary dictates that the overarching task of AGI alignment verification is fundamentally and inescapably undecidable. ■\blacksquare
